title: Industrial applications of electrolysis
competency: Explain how electrolysis is used to extract and refine metals, electroplate, and make nonmetals and compounds.

keywords.def: A mineral from which a metal can be extracted economically.
A naturally occurring material that contains a metal or its compound.
Purifying a metal by electrolysis: impure anode, pure cathode, salt solution.
Coating an object (the cathode) with a thin layer of metal by electrolysis.
Insoluble impurities (Ag, Au, Pt) that settle under the anode during refining.
Electrolysis of brine to make chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

en.text: Metals less reactive than carbon are extracted by heating their ores with carbon. Very reactive metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds, because no cheap chemical reducing agent is strong enough. Aluminium comes from molten Al₂O₃: Al³⁺ is reduced at the cathode and O²⁻ is oxidized to O₂ at the anode.

en.text: In electrorefining, impure metal is the anode, a thin sheet of pure metal is the cathode and a salt of the metal is the electrolyte. The metal dissolves from the anode and deposits pure on the cathode; less active impurities fall as anode mud. In electroplating, the object to be coated is the cathode, the plating metal is the anode, and its salt is the electrolyte.

en.text: Electrolysis also makes nonmetals and compounds. In the chlor-alkali process, brine gives chlorine at the anode and hydrogen with hydroxide at the cathode, so sodium hydroxide forms. Fluorine is made from molten KF and HF, and water with a little added electrolyte gives hydrogen and oxygen.
